title: Standard deviation in investing
subtitle: The mathematical tool that precisely measures volatility
openingQuestion: Fund A averages 10%/year with a 5% standard deviation. Fund B also averages 10%/year but with a 20% standard deviation. Which fund is 'easier to predict'?
openingOptions: Cannot be compared without a longer observation period
Both are the same since the average return is identical
Fund A - a lower standard deviation means actual yearly returns cluster closer to the average, with fewer surprises
Fund B, because its standard deviation is higher
explanation: Standard deviation precisely measures, in a single number, how dispersed returns are around their average. Two assets with the same expected return but different standard deviations carry very different risk levels: a lower standard deviation means the actual outcome is less 'surprising' year to year.

diagram.label: Measure the dispersion around that value

realWorldExample.company: Comparing a bond fund and a stock fund
realWorldExample.description: A government bond fund usually has an annual return standard deviation of just 2-5%, while a growth stock fund can reach 15-25% - clearly reflecting the difference in risk between the two asset types.

quiz.question: In a normal distribution, roughly what percentage of outcomes fall within ±1 standard deviation of the average?
options: About 50%, since one standard deviation splits the distribution in half
About 68% - following the 68-95-99.7 rule of a normal distribution
Cannot be determined without actual return data
100%, since every observation falls within one standard deviation
quiz.explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule: if returns are normally distributed, about 68% of observations fall within ±1 standard deviation, 95% within ±2, and 99.7% within ±3.

quiz.question: If an asset's return distribution doesn't follow a normal distribution (it has "fat tails" - a higher probability of extreme events than predicted), is standard deviation alone enough to measure risk?
options: Standard deviation alone is fine for every asset type in every situation
Yes, standard deviation always accurately reflects every kind of asset risk
A normal distribution always holds true for every financial asset that exists
No - it understates the probability of extreme events, so add VaR too
quiz.explanation: This is an important limitation many economists (like Nassim Taleb with his "Black Swan" concept) have pointed out: real financial markets tend to have far more extreme events than a normal distribution predicts.

quiz.question: What does an asset's standard deviation measure?
options: The dispersion of returns around the average value
The gap between the highest and lowest return
The probability that asset loses money in any given year
The average growth rate of the asset across the years
quiz.explanation: It measures the width of the distribution, not its direction. Two assets with the same 10% average return but standard deviations of 5% and 25% deliver completely different experiences for the holder.

quiz.question: Average return of 8%, standard deviation of 15%. What range contains roughly 68% of years?
options: From 0% to 16% (= 8% ± 8%, using the wrong number)
From −7% to 23% (= 8% ± 15% standard deviation)
From −15% to 15% (using only the standard deviation)
From 8% to 23% (counting only the upside)
quiz.explanation: In a normal distribution, one standard deviation around the average contains 68% of observations. The −7% figure shows that even an asset with a decent expected return still has fairly frequent negative years.

quiz.question: Why does standard deviation understate the real risk of financial markets?
options: Because it completely ignores the downside portion of volatility
Because it can only be calculated with over ten years of data
Because actual returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution
Because it's calculated on closing prices rather than intraday prices
quiz.explanation: Major crashes happen far more often than a normal distribution predicts. Events the model calls a once-in-ten-thousand-years occurrence have shown up several times in just recent decades.

keyTakeaways: Standard deviation: the precise mathematical tool for measuring return dispersion
Two assets with the same average return but different standard deviations carry very different risk
The 68-95-99.7 rule helps estimate the probability of real-world return scenarios

practicePrompt.question: You want to quantify a stock's volatility with a specific number (not just a qualitative description like 'very volatile' or 'stable'), based on 3 years of monthly return history. What mathematical tool is used to calculate this number?
options: Beta, since it's the only tool that measures a stock's degree of volatility
Standard deviation measures the dispersion of returns around the average
Correlation, since it's the tool that measures an individual asset's price swings
No mathematical tool can precisely quantify volatility, only qualitative estimation is possible
practicePrompt.explanation: Standard deviation: the precise mathematical tool for measuring return dispersion around the average. This is the most common way to quantify volatility in finance - the larger the standard deviation, the more widely dispersed the returns, and the more the asset swings.

application.title: Look up a fund's standard deviation
application.message: The lesson already showed how to read the standard deviation on a real fund's factsheet (for example VESAF) - see the section above. Now download the factsheet of a fund you're interested in and find that number yourself.
application.secondary: This number often gets overlooked, but it says a lot about how much 'surprise' you should expect.

sections.text: Standard deviation is the mathematical tool that turns the concept of "volatility" into a precise number - measuring how dispersed returns are around their average. Two assets with the same expected return but different standard deviations carry very different risk levels: a lower standard deviation means the actual outcome is less "surprising" from year to year.

If an asset's returns follow a normal distribution, about 68% of outcomes fall within ±1 standard deviation of the average, 95% fall within ±2, and 99.7% fall within ±3. This is a basic statistical rule widely used in finance to estimate the probability of return scenarios. For example, a government bond fund typically has an annual return standard deviation of just 2-5%, while a growth stock fund can reach 15-25% - clearly reflecting the difference in risk.

The problem is that real financial markets don't always follow a normal distribution - many assets have "fat tails", meaning the probability of an extreme event (a market crash, a crisis) is much higher than a normal distribution predicts. Nassim Taleb calls these events "Black Swans". Relying on standard deviation alone to measure risk can lead an investor to UNDERSTATE the probability of major shocks - other tools such as Value at Risk or stress testing need to be added.

items: Standard deviation precisely quantifies how dispersed returns are
The 68-95-99.7 rule helps estimate the probability of return scenarios
Government bonds: low standard deviation (2-5%); growth stocks: high (15-25%)
Assets with "fat tails" cause plain standard deviation to understate extreme risk

sections.text: How to read standard deviation on a real fund factsheet

items: Vietnamese open-ended fund factsheets (VESAF, VEOF, SSI-SCA...) usually publish an annual "Standard Deviation" figure alongside the average return - this measures how much returns swing year to year, not the return itself

Two funds with the same average return but different standard deviations: the fund with lower standard deviation is more trustworthy, since its returns are steadier year to year, rather than swinging between very high and very low years
VESAF averaged 22.9%/year (over 5 years) - this figure alone doesn't tell you about stability; it needs to be set beside the standard deviation for a full assessment

sections.label: How to look this up yourself
sections.text: Open a fund's PDF factsheet (downloadable from the fund manager's website, e.g. VinaCapital, SSIAM), find the "Statistics" section, and compare the standard deviation between 2 funds with a similar expected return.

lines: Standard deviation gives you a number - but that number is only correct if the real world behaves the way the model assumes.
